title: Start selling before you need the money · hancrafted
description: Why sales must start long before revenue is needed, shown on a month-by-month cashflow board, and the first concrete steps to build a sales pipeline: find your zero-cash month, start a lead list, make first contact, and track your conversion rate and sales cycle.

Watch your cashflow Costs come first A startup's first expenses, such as company setup and the founders' living costs, arise before it has users or income. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, A Student's Guide to Startups: Startup Funding ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com Promised money arrives late Closing an investor takes longer than expected even after a yes, and one angel took months to pay. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, A Student's Guide to Startups: Startup Funding ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com Hiring ahead does not pay itself There is little connection between how much a startup spends and how fast it grows, so rising costs do not bring revenue forward. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Default Alive or Default Dead? ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com
Why sales is more than just selling No speaker notes for this Slide.

Sales is more than selling Your guess of the customer is wrong A founder's initial model of users is always inaccurate, even if the founder is one of them; direct contact is what corrects it. 1 Sources (1) Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com Investors read the team Among 885 venture capitalists the management team was the most-cited important factor (95%), ahead of product and market. That a signed letter of intent or a full pipeline raises trust is an inference: no study tests them directly. 1 Sources (1) Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev, How Do Venture Capitalists Make Decisions? ( opens in a new tab ) nber.org Scale after you find the process Premature scaling of sales and marketing is the leading cause of cash loss in a startup; scale after the founders have found a repeatable sales model. 1 Sources (1) Blank, It Must Be A Marketing Problem ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com
How to start doing sales No speaker notes for this Slide.

Stages of sale Delivery is not payment With no contract term, interest on a late B2B payment starts only 30 days after the invoice is received, and contract terms may run up to 60 days. 1 Sources (1) European Parliament and Council, Directive 2011/7/EU on combating late payment in commercial transactions ( opens in a new tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu Acceptance adds time An acceptance or verification step can add up to 30 more days before the payment period starts. 1 Sources (1) European Parliament and Council, Directive 2011/7/EU on combating late payment in commercial transactions ( opens in a new tab ) eur-lex.europa.eu

Pipeline tools in practice Slipping deals convert worse In one vendor dataset, deals that slip late in the cycle convert worse, and winning deals involved decision makers early. 1 Sources (1) Ebsta and Pavilion, GTM Benchmarks Report ( opens in a new tab ) benchmarks.ebsta.com

How marketing feeds the pipeline Customers do not arrive on their own “You can’t wait for users to come to you. You have to go out and get them”; getting users is a gradual process. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com

Watch your cashflow, revenue pulled in Predicted revenue does not count Revenue that is only predicted is discounted by investors, and founders who rely on raising more money often find that assumption false. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Default Alive or Default Dead? ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com

What is a sales pipeline Rates differ per stage In one dataset the MQL-to-SQL rate was 68 percent beside a 19 percent win rate. 1 Inference, not a finding: stage definitions may differ per company, so rates may not be comparable across companies. Sources (1) Ebsta and Pavilion, GTM Benchmarks Report ( opens in a new tab ) benchmarks.ebsta.com

Pipeline by the numbers Measured, one dataset In a dataset of 655 thousand opportunities across 387 companies, the new-customer win rate was 19 percent, the sales cycle 91 days and 8 stakeholders per deal; for expansion sales to existing customers it was 45 percent, 52 days and 5 stakeholders. 1 Sources (1) Ebsta and Pavilion, GTM Benchmarks Report ( opens in a new tab ) benchmarks.ebsta.com Most losses are no decision An analysis of more than 2.5 million sales conversations found that 40 to 60 percent of deals are lost to buyers who intend to buy but never act. 1 Sources (1) Dixon and McKenna, Stop Losing Sales to Customer Indecision (Harvard Business Review) ( opens in a new tab ) hbr.org The buyer is a group A Gartner survey of 632 B2B buyers describes buying groups of five to 16 people, and 74 percent of buyer teams showed unhealthy conflict. 1 Sources (1) Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate "Unhealthy Conflict" During The Decision Process ( opens in a new tab ) gartner.com

Why it takes time to ramp up You search before you execute A startup is a temporary organization designed to search for a repeatable and scalable business model; the facts a pipeline depends on are found in conversations with customers. 1 Sources (1) Steve Blank, The Customer Development Manifesto ( opens in a new tab ) steveblank.com Metrics lag by the cycle A conversion figure for recent leads looks worse than the long-run value because those leads have not yet gone through a full sales cycle. 1 Sources (1) Mark Roberge, The Science of Scaling ( opens in a new tab ) f.hubspotusercontent10.net Codify after you learn Roberge advises codifying the go-to-market playbook only after the learning, and proving scalable unit economics before aggressively hiring salespeople. 1 Sources (1) Mark Roberge, The Science of Scaling ( opens in a new tab ) f.hubspotusercontent10.net

Watch your cashflow, "Start when?" Worry early The test is whether a company reaches profitability on its remaining money at current expenses and growth; worrying too early is cheap and worrying too late is dangerous. 1 Sources (1) Paul Graham, Default Alive or Default Dead? ( opens in a new tab ) paulgraham.com

script.text: This panel shows the speaker notes and voice script for the Slide you are reading, and follows you as you scroll. Press Alt+N to open or close it.

Why watching cashflow is mission critical 0:00 – 0:20 Hook bankrupt in March a million in April one month off Picture a company that goes bankrupt in March. Its biggest deal, a million dollars, lands in April. The numbers were fine. The timing was one month off. I want to show you why that happens, and what you do about it before it happens to you. 0:20 – 0:37 Today's route four steps your cash what sales is how to start start when? We take four steps today. First, you see your cash. Second, you see what sales really is. Third, you learn how to start. Fourth, you see why a pipeline takes time to build. Then one question decides it all: start when?

Watch your cashflow 0:00 – 0:24 Read the board one column per month cash cost revenue left to right Here is the board. One column per month. Yellow notes are cash, red notes are cost, green notes are revenue. In January you have a hundred thousand dollars and spend fifty thousand. In February you have fifty thousand and spend fifty thousand again. Revenue shows up only in April. Walk it month by month, left to right. 0:24 – 0:45 Zero-cash month cash reads zero March bankrupt the number you need Look at the cash note after February. It reads zero. March has a cost note and nothing to pay it with. So you stamp the board: bankrupt. That month, the one where cash hits zero, is the number you need to find. Everything else on this board is secondary. 0:45 – 1:02 First actionable build your own board mark your zero-cash month sticky notes spreadsheet So here is your first task. Build this board for your own company. One column per month. Cash, cost, revenue. Fill it in honestly, then mark your zero-cash month. Pen and sticky notes are enough. A spreadsheet works too. 1:02 – 1:15 Right deal, wrong month the million is real late revenue timing not total Notice what is not wrong here. The million dollars is real. The customer is real. The revenue is simply late. It is the timing that kills the company, not the total.

Why sales is more than just selling 0:00 – 0:18 Sales pays before revenue sales revenue three payoffs Now the second idea. Most founders think sales gives you revenue, and only revenue. But selling pays you back long before the first invoice is paid. It pays in three other ways, and we will put each one on the board.

Sales is more than selling 0:00 – 0:23 Market insight wrong buyer build already paid for price of skipping early sales The first note: market insight. Look at your offer. Suppose it is aimed at the wrong buyer. You will not see that on the board. You will see it after the build is paid for. The money is gone, and the offer still has to change. That is the price of skipping early sales. 0:23 – 0:42 Trust customers and investors an early deal paid attention or money faith The second note: trust. Customers and investors both trust a company that has already sold something. An early deal, even a small one, says that someone paid attention, or paid money. A company with nothing sold asks them to take it on faith. 0:42 – 0:59 Repeatable process which steps work write it down first sales hire The third note: a repeatable process. When you sell yourself, you see which steps work, and in which order. Write that down. It becomes the process you can later hand to a first sales hire, instead of handing over a hope. 0:59 – 1:10 Converge on trust three notes three arrows a company others dare to bet on Three notes, three arrows, one place they end. A company others dare to bet on. That is what early selling builds, long before it builds revenue.

How to start doing sales 0:00 – 0:12 From idea to first step the practical part stages of a sale what first same board Now the practical part. What are the stages of a sale? And what do you do first? We stay on the same board, only the notes change.

Stages of sale 0:00 – 0:12 Three stages leads opportunities closing left to right some drop out A sale has three stages. Leads, opportunities, closing. Every customer you will ever win walks this path, left to right. Some drop out on the way. That is normal. 0:12 – 0:31 Second actionable, lead list lead generation now research list of potential customers add names every week Your second task sits under leads. Start lead generation now. Research who could buy from you, and write them in a list. Then keep the list alive. Add names every week. A list of potential customers is the cheapest asset you can build today. 0:31 – 0:49 Third actionable, first contact cold call inbound network introduction name to opportunity Your third task is the first contact. Call a name from your list, cold. Answer an inbound message. Ask someone in your network for an introduction. Any of the three works. The point is that contact turns a name into an opportunity. 0:49 – 1:05 Opportunities are the work follow up material meetings negotiate contract An opportunity is where the work begins. Someone is interested, and now you follow up. You send material, you hold meetings, you negotiate. Interest is only the start. Closing is where the customer agrees to a contract. 1:05 – 1:24 Lag after the deal faint note deliver invoice wait for payment cash later still And look at the faint note after closing. Even a signed deal does not put cash in the bank. First you deliver, then you invoice, then you wait for payment. The cash arrives later still, so the board needs to count that wait too.

Pipeline tools in practice 0:00 – 0:26 One board for all deals one place one note per deal five columns company and value total on top Now you need one place for all your deals. Draw a board. Each deal is one note, and each note sits in one column: lead in, contact made, needs defined, proposal made, negotiations started. The company name and the value are on the note. The total sits on top of each column. You see your whole pipeline at a glance. 0:26 – 0:45 Fourth actionable, track deals simple pipeline spreadsheet or free tool current not clever measure it Here is your fourth task. Track every deal in a simple pipeline. Start with a spreadsheet or a free tool. It does not need to be clever. It needs to be current. Then you can measure it, and we come to that in a minute. 0:45 – 1:01 Move or drop one note moves do not hope decide push forward or drop Watch one note move from one column to the next. That is what you want. If a deal does not move, you do not hope. You decide. Push it forward, or drop it and free your attention.

How marketing feeds the pipeline 0:00 – 0:14 Volume funnel many people at once a few raise a hand high volume small yield Marketing works like a funnel. It speaks to many people at once, and a few of them raise a hand. High volume, small yield. That is how it is supposed to work. 0:14 – 0:31 Enter a defined stage a lead not a customer inbound lead sales makes contact fills and works A person who raises a hand does not become a customer. They become a lead in one defined stage of your pipeline, for example an inbound lead. Only then does sales make contact. Marketing fills the pipeline, and sales works it. 0:31 – 0:48 You do not need it first no campaign first no budget network and phone first contact this week So do not park your first task behind a campaign. You have no budget and no audience yet. You do have a network and a phone. Make your first contact this week, and let the funnel come later.

Watch your cashflow, revenue pulled in 0:00 – 0:17 Same board, earlier revenue first board same costs revenue back to February stays positive no stamp Now back to our first board. Same notes, same costs. This time, I drag April's revenue back two months, to February. The cash note after February no longer reads zero. It stays positive. No bankrupt stamp. The story flips. 0:17 – 0:33 Not more, earlier not a cent more revenue moved to the costs the whole game earlier Look at what changed. The company did not earn a cent more. Its revenue moved to the month where the costs were. That is the whole game. You do not need more revenue. You need revenue earlier. 0:33 – 0:44 How it moves not by wishing earlier sales sales takes time next part But revenue does not move by wishing. Earlier revenue only comes from earlier sales. And sales takes time. That is why the next part is about time.

Why building an effective sales pipeline takes time 0:00 – 0:13 Not a switch not a switch build measure tune weeks A pipeline is not a switch you flip when the money runs low. You build it. You measure it. You tune it. And each of those takes weeks before it works.

What is a sales pipeline 0:00 – 0:12 Funnel three numbers the funnel volume per stage Three numbers describe a pipeline. The first is the funnel itself. Take each stage of the sale and count how much volume sits in it right now. 0:12 – 0:26 Conversion rate how many reach the next stage attractiveness low rate The second is the conversion rate. Out of everyone in one stage, how many reach the next? It tells you how attractive your offering is. A low rate means people look and walk away. 0:26 – 0:43 Sales cycle days from first contact to close efficiency money stuck The third is the sales cycle. Count the days from first contact to a closed deal, or to a paid invoice. It tells you how efficient you are. A long cycle means your money is stuck on the way. 0:43 – 0:58 Fourth actionable, measure fourth task write down conversion rate and sales cycle plan backwards That is why your fourth task includes measuring. From your first deals on, write down your conversion rate and your sales cycle. Two numbers. You will need both to plan backwards from your zero-cash month.

Pipeline by the numbers 0:00 – 0:11 Illustration a complex sale illustration not benchmark your numbers differ Here is an example of a complex sale. It is an illustration, not a benchmark. Your numbers will differ. But it shows how the arithmetic behaves. 0:11 – 0:27 Ratios multiply three to one nine to one twenty-seven leads per deal Three leads become one opportunity. Nine opportunities become one deal. Multiply it out and you need twenty-seven leads for a single deal. Small ratios at each stage add up to a very big number at the top. 0:27 – 0:45 Time adds up two weeks six months three months most of a year Now the time. Two weeks for the first stage. Six months for the second. Three months for the third. Add them up and revenue lands most of a year after the first contact. A year is longer than most founders' cash. 0:45 – 0:59 Measured sits beside it a real dataset shorter cycle your own numbers Beside it sits a real, measured dataset. Its cycle is much shorter than the illustration's. Still, it is one dataset from other companies. Your own numbers will tell you more than any of these. 0:59 – 1:13 So fill early many leads in long wait out start filling now Many leads go in. A long wait comes out. If that is true for you, you have only one move. Start filling the pipeline now, while you still have cash to wait with.

Why it takes time to ramp up 0:00 – 0:20 Preparation sales deck pricing demo proposal contract takes longer than you think The first note is preparation. A sales deck. Pricing. An offering and a business model. A demo, meeting slides, a proposal. A contract, with compliance and legal covered. All of this has to exist before the first deal can close. Writing it takes longer than you think. 0:20 – 0:45 Unknown market who what they pay which problem months not days the clock runs The second note is the unknown market. Who is your customer? What will they pay? Which problem do they truly need solved? Until you know, every number on the cashflow board is a guess. Price, volume, timing: each rests on those three answers. The answers take months, not days. The clock on your cash keeps running meanwhile. 0:45 – 1:00 Unknown metrics conversion rate and sales cycle unknown plan backwards only by selling The third note is unknown metrics. At the start you do not know your conversion rate or your sales cycle. You need both to plan backwards from your cash. And you only get them by selling. 1:00 – 1:15 No shortcut preparation market metrics real time start early Preparation, market, metrics. Each of the three takes real time, and there is no shortcut through any of them. You cannot rush them once the money is short. You can only start them early.

Start before you need the money 0:00 – 0:18 Back to the board the board one last time quarters Q1 to Q4 revenue in the third quarter one question Let us go back to the board one last time. Now with four quarter columns, Q1 to Q4. Cash, cost and revenue as before. Revenue arrives only in the third quarter. And the board has been asking one question all along.

Watch your cashflow, "Start when?" 0:00 – 0:15 Start when arrow from Q3 back to Q1 not when the money runs low the first column right now Look at the arrow from Q3 back to Q1. It says: start when? Not when the money runs low. By then, the revenue is already months away. The right moment is the first column. Right now. 0:15 – 0:31 Learning goal sales before revenue is needed revenue trails costs how the clock runs So here is the point of this talk. Sales must start long before revenue is needed, because revenue trails costs. Always. It is not a sign of a bad company. It is how the clock runs. 0:31 – 0:50 Your four steps cashflow view lead list first contact track deals conversion rate sales cycle Your four steps. One: build your cashflow view and find your zero-cash month. Two: keep a lead list, and add to it. Three: make first contact, by cold call, inbound or network. Four: track your deals, and measure your conversion rate and your sales cycle. 0:50 – 1:05 This week pick the first step draw the board find the month how early to start You do not have to do all four today. Pick the first one and do it this week. Draw the board, find the month, and you will know exactly how early you have to start.
